utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, our next witness is Admiral Vlade Nonkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Nonkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You'll now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Admiral. Admiral, can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly about your military career, when you completed the military academy, and what posts you held.

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: As for the military naval academy, I graduated in 1965. I sailed on ships for ten years. Then I taught at the navy teaching centre, then I was commander of a logistics base, one, and another one. And the last seven years of my career I spent in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia as chief of administration for the navy, or rather, the sector for the navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is the highest rank you held in the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Vice-admiral.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Vice-admiral. Can you tell us if we compare this to ranks in the army, what army rank would correspond to vice-admiral if it is possible to classify it that way?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: It is simply possible, that is lieutenant-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what duties did you discharge in 1998 and 1999? You said that you spent the last seven years of your career in the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of sector for navy, or rather, assistant Chief of Staff of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia for navy and also chief of navy sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I just have to ask you that we pause between question and answer so that the interpreters catch up and they manage to clearly interpret the questions and the answers. As chief of sector, as chief of navy sector, or rather, assistant Chief of Staff for the navy, did you attend collegium meetings that the Chief of Staff had?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were a permanent member of the collegium, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to go through a few collegium meetings from 1998 with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that purpose could the witness please be shown Defence Exhibit 3D657. Your Honour, this is the collegium of the 10th of April, 1998, and could you please display page 16 in the B/C/S and page 2 in the English text. The lower part of the page, please, in B/C/S. Could that please be displayed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Admiral, at this collegium meeting, like at many others, the situation was reviewed concerning developments in Kosovo. Do you remember what was discussed on this occasion and what General Ojdanic's participation in the discussion was?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it would be too broad-based to go into everything that was discussed. I would just like to focus on the main statements made, if I can put it that way, and General Ojdanic's remarks. I think that the essence of this was, as he said, that the problem of Kosovo cannot be resolved through war, but rather that it has to be resolved through politics and diplomacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at that time, which is already the spring of 1998, and the KLA terrorist forces were on the rise, was there a pressure that was felt that the army should in a way be involved in resolving the problems in connection with terrorist activities in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what pressure you're referring to, I mean pressure on the part of the people or the population in Kosovo or members of the collegium of the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I wasn't specific enough, but at that time was one of the options considered the one that had to do with the MUP not being able to deal with terrorism on it own and that the army would have to get involved?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there were some discussions -- well, not having the army involved, but having them take a more active position. This was a free discussion, so to speak, and perhaps it was stated, stated, if I can put it that way, that if this trend were continue in terms of terrorist activity in Kosovo, that probably even the MUP will not be able to handle all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the position of the international community and General Ojdanic's view?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that precisely at this collegium General Ojdanic pointed out that the international community in this situation as it was, at that point in time, would not take a favourable view if the army were to directly oppose the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to draw your attention to a particular section of General Ojdanic's remarks, page 16, paragraph 3 in B/C/S, when he says: "I think," in English by the way it is around the middle of the first paragraph. He says: "I think that the method of Albanians in terms of further pressures is going to be continuing with this terrorist activity because that has yielded result. This activity will gradually increase, the aim being for them to become so strong that they cannot objectively be opposed by the MUP forces as the only competent and internationally recognised force for confronting terrorist groups." General -- sorry, Admiral, rather, as the discussion continued, in General Ojdanic's view what was necessary in order for the Army of Yugoslavia to do something, prepare something, or address the state leadership in terms of developments that were yet to ensue?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in terms of these forecasts and assessments and these discussions, if I can put this in very concise terms, the Supreme Defence Council should be provided with an objective picture in terms of what the abilities of the military were, so that on the basis of this picture, if I can put it that way, the state leadership were to make realistic decisions on the basis of the objective possibilities of the army and the country as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 17 in B/C/S, paragraph 1, and in English, page 2, the last paragraph in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: It's the last few lines when General Ojdanic says: "That is going to be a good indicator to have political and state decisions based on the realistic abilities of this army and this country naturally with the assumption that the mobilisation carried out by this state will not face the same problems it has had in this unfortunate war." And the last sentence: "Nobody will support our force as far as Kosovo is concerned." Admiral --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could counsel please just indicate clearly where this is in the English part of e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last page, or rather, the last four or five lines on page 2. They tell me it's the last seven lines if that means anything as far as Mr. Stamp is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Admiral, you said that this was an open, frank discussion. This discussion continued during the ensuing period at collegium meetings of the General Staff as the situation developed and as the terrorist forces stepped-up their activity?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to have 3D658 displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is the collegium of the 17th of April, 1998, B/C/S page 46, English page 2. Please, in B/C/S the lower part of page 46. In English the same thing, the lower part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Admiral, a few moments ago you talked about this proposal made by General Ojdanic at the previous collegium meeting; however, now I think it was defined somewhat better, so could you please give us your comments -- actually, General Ojdanic says: "To have our state leadership make decisions that would be realistic and optimal as much as possible in the interests of both the people and the state, I judge that it is our obligation, and that is the only thing I would like to propose, to send immediately a brief report to the VSO on the situation with regard to the VJ's combat-readiness and capacity where we would clearly describe what General Kosta has talked about." Admiral, first I'll ask you who General Kosta is?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Kosta Arsenovic, Lieutenant-General Arsenovic, assistant Chief of General Staff for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General Arsenovic spoke at this collegium meeting. Can you tell the Trial Chamber briefly what the essence was?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: The essence of his remarks was that he portrayed through tables, if I can put it that way, the smallest and the biggest calibres of weapons. As for ammunition he said what the resources were in terms of fuel, clothing, and so on and so forth, practically he gave us all the data from his line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And what were his conclusions? What was it that he warned about?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no one had to make any conclusions whatsoever. It was so clear, this picture, how much the Army of Yugoslavia could take in terms of war days, as we say. Yes, I understand what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us in greater detail how many days the Army of Yugoslavia could take, how long?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that collegium we did not specify whether it was five or ten days, but at any rate our estimates as to how long realistically the struggle against terrorism could take in Kosovo, that would take far greater amounts of materiel and equipment than was shown in the tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I would now like you to look at paragraph 2 where General Ojdanic says: "This is our situation and our capacity, and I'm convinced that after we've realised this people will think differently about any possible war option which will end. I must, I'm not a skeptic, I was never afraid in my life, but to go into a war, I don't agree with the statements made here that something can be finished in two days." Admiral, if I'm right, this is precisely -- or this is rather similar to what General Arsenovic himself presented. But now I would like you to explain to us how you understand this passage in what General Ojdanic said, where he says: "The moment this happens the air force will cease to exist, a decision will be made to prohibit all its flights, and the variety -- the option for 700 ethnically clean villages in Kosovo and Metohija, if we divide -- if we allot just one company per each such settlement, how many companies, how many battalions it would take, how many brigades," and so on. My first question regarding this is: What is General Ojdanic talking about when he's talking about 700 ethnically clean settlements in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, indubitably he's talking about the 700 ethnically clean settlements where Serbs lived. So since we're talking about clean settlements, the army had no ability whatsoever to rely on the people, on the territory, and that is why he said that if only one company, one small company, were to be assigned to each such settlement, the question would be how many battalions, brigades, and so on it would require for the Army of Yugoslavia to be able to cope with all the troubles in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move on to the next page in B/C/S. And the next page in English as well. It's the first paragraph in both version sincere midway through this passage where General Ojdanic says: "But we have to tell the state leadership the truth that our materiel reserves are so exhausted that we are not capable that because of this we cannot wage a long-lasting war, that all our resources are like -- I hope that after this their reasoning of those who may be out of touch with all of this will be much more realistic and these decisions which they will consequently make will be closer to the views of those of us who are sitting here."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Admiral, my question to you: The General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia was aware of the fact that the Army of Yugoslavia cannot and need not join the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you, for the avoidance of any doubt, make it clear which war you're referring to, war with whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we're still referring to the war against the terrorism in Kosovo, direct involvement of the army in the clashes with the terrorists. And probably in the background, given the situation and the developments, perhaps a war at a larger scale was also meant, but let me repeat the focus at this moment was on direct involvement of the army in the war against terrorism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in just a few words can you summarize for us the options presented by Generals Bane and Aco.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this was a term of endearment, a nickname, that's Bane, an intelligence officer, and Aco, Aco was Aleksandar Dimitrijevic, the chief of the security administration. Well, the options were rather broad and they were both in the sphere of politics. So they took into account the international community, the international factor, various pressures, what the conditions that were placed upon us, what we should do, but these two options were quite similar, both in the sphere of politics. And of course there was a certain threat of a military intervention present there, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now could we please have yet another collegium shown to the witness, and that's the last collegium meeting, that's 3D659. This is the collegium meeting of the 4th of May, 1998. And could the witness please be shown page 8 in B/C/S and page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Admiral, at the end of this paragraph, that's the first paragraph in what General Ojdanic said, that's in both versions on this page, General Ojdanic repeats here that the leadership should be told what the army was capable of doing if it turns out that the war in Kosovo is inevitable. And now I would like to focus on the second paragraph in his intervention where he says: "I repeat what I have already said several times and what you have also confirmed several times, that the shortest and fastest way to lose Kosovo is by war, precisely because nobody will allow us to resolve that on our own, faced on one side, on the other side with the secessionist movement in Kosovo and Metohija." A little while ago when Judge Bonomy asked you a question about the options that were discussed at the previous collegium meeting you said that this is what General Milovanovic and General Dimitrijevic said. They both talked about the situation in Kosovo from a broader international aspect, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When General Ojdanic said nobody will allow us to resolve that on our own, who is he talking about?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that General Ojdanic is referring to the international community, that they would not allow us, they would not take a favourable view of that if we were to decide to deploy the army using our own decision-making and our own chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that what Dimitrijevic and Milovanovic wanted to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I think that here this is a proposal, a view, made by General Ojdanic. So this is the collegium of the 4th of May. What we were talking about General Dimitrijevic, that was on the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. What I'm trying to be clear about is what it was that he and Milovanovic suggested, which was rejected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, they did not make any proposals about the use of the army. They merely presented their view, security assessment, a security and intelligence assessment, in light of certain thoughts on the part of the international community and certain conditions that were imposed, but they did not make any proposals as to what the army should do. So this collegium has nothing to do with what they had said at the previous one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you finished with this page now, Mr. Visnjic, or have you more from this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question relating to this page. The last few lines on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at where General Ojdanic says: "General Borovic is absolutely right that those Serbs down there are at present unprotected. At this moment, forces of the MUP of Serbia are responsible for their protection; whether they're doing this and how, that is another matter, and whether there are enough of them to be able to perform all those tasks in a proper manner." Admiral, do you know about what General Ojdanic was thinking regarding the role the army was to play in protecting the population?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at this collegium meeting it is quite clear that General Ojdanic was trying to avoid at any cost using the Army of Yugoslavia in Kosovo. I think that General Borovic is actually talking about some Serbs, unprotected villages, and so on, and General Ojdanic says that in this situation the only competent force to deal with this problem is the MUP of Serbia. And now another issue is whether it was capable to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am done with this collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'd briefly like to go back to 3D658, please, if we could have that on the screen, and it's page 2 in the English. I think it was page 46, was it, in B/C/S. It's enough at the moment if you just let me see the English version. Thank you. Yeah. The sentence that aroused my interest here says this, and this is General Ojdanic speaking: "I think that all indicators mentioned today and not only today confirm that the international community and its relevant institutions are set to make the FRY resolve the status of Kosovo by one of the two current options which we heard today from General Bane and General Aco." Now, what were these two current options?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that none of the options was such that it proposed the use of our forces, but as far as I can remember one of the options was that the international community would be exerting pressure on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to try and find a political settlement for the crisis in Kosovo. And there would be some other demands that would be made, for instance, to recognise the referendum that had been carried out in Kosovo. It is well-known that the president of the state and -- other elections were also carried out and also another option was that the referendum in Serbia would also be taken into account and recognised. And also in solving this situation in Kosovo and Metohija, the mediation of the international community had to be accepted and I think that mention was made of an international force was to be brought to Kosovo, NATO force, not just international force, and that this option -- and that the terrorism in Kosovo would be supported, that the terrorists would be armed and equipped, and that would require in one way or another for the Army of Yugoslavia to be used. As far as I can remember this debate or the intervention by General Dimitrijevic, that was the first option. And there was also the threat of a more comprehensive set of sanctions that would be in force for six months. This -- the second option was a bit milder, selective sanctions for the duration of six months were envisaged. Again, the presence of the international factor in trying to find a settlement for the political crisis, possible bringing of troops in Kosovo, and again support for terrorism. But I remember that this second option, that if such conditioning were to be in place, that again the Army of Yugoslavia would have to be engaged. And I think that in accordance with those two options that were presented, I think that General Ojdanic just mentioned them in passing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, or rather, I would like to make a proposal to amend this exhibit. The same document page 11, let's try to agree on the nominal pages in the B/C/S, pages 11 through 16, that's where we find General Milovanovic's contribution from page 24 to page 29 we see the contribution of General Dimitrijevic. What I can do is ask the CLSS to translate both documents, both portions of the document, rather, and then with your approval, Your Honours, we might try to additionally tender that. I think this will make the situation easier for everyone for further analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... The Admiral has explained the position. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Admiral, a while ago we looked at all these documents and several times we returned to the materiel situation of the VJ, or rather, its ability or inability to carry out some of its legal obligations. You looked at the overall budget of the VJ for 1998 and 1999, did you not? First of all, can you tell us if this was one of your responsibilities that stemmed from your job, your position? Can you tell us more about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of my responsibilities, to remain involved in the drafting of what we used to call the annual budget plan, assignment and the financing of the VJ, and I was in charge of this budgetary plan for the navy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I want to take a closer look at the time-frame. When does one start planning a military budget?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: This normally starts sometime around early September each year --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The plan and the preparations of the budget might well be within his -- his job description, but that is not within the 65 ter describing what he would testify about. I am taken by surprise by this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, paragraph 3 of the 65 ter says: "Witness will testify about planning in the General Staff of the VJ throughout 1998 and 1999." I think that is precisely what the witness started telling us about; otherwise, I wasn't going to dwell on this for too long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, does that not cover the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would submit no. I would suggest that this is much too vague to cover the preparation of the budget. If he's just going to deal with it on its face and move on, then perhaps he could, but we have not looked into anything dealing with the budget in preparation for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, please continue and we'll hear if there is particular prejudice caused in due course, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So you told us that the planning stage begins around early September each year?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When is the final decision taken on the budget, at what time?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: The final decision is made by the federal government normally sometime in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: December. All right. The budget, when the budget is planned, I mean, it refers to all the planned activities of the army, we're talking about the military budget for the following year, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. You looked at the 1998 budget and the 1999 budget. Can you tell us if there were any substantial differences between the planning for these two budgets in relation to both years?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Virtually no difference. It was slightly bigger in relation to 1999 because of some degree of inflation, but this wasn't the only reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If you could please just explain once more. You said it was bigger because there was a certain degree of inflation, but not the entire inflation was included in this enlargement, so to speak, of the budget?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me phrase this differently. Are you telling us that the 1999 budget was nominally bigger than the 1998 budget, but still smaller than the inflation grade at the time, the inflation rate?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When a budget is planned by an army, is there a difference normally between the wartime budget and the peacetime budget or is no distinction made along these lines?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: There should be a distinction, but we never planned for a wartime budget; we continued to plan a peacetime budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the budget was normally adopted sometime late in December. In lately December and early January, what was the situation concerning the NATO forces around the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I mean here specifically your own area, the navy?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please have Defence Exhibit 3D685 prepared for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to this exhibit straight off.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you probably remember this is the intelligence and security assessment dated February 1999. Can we please have page 27 in the B/C/S. The English reference is 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Admiral, sometime early in 1999, was there an increase or greater concentration of NATO forces around the FRY?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in relation to the preceding period, there was a greater concentration of NATO's navy in the Adriatic, given the fact that there were certain activities that were being carried out at the time. There were preparations for political negotiations on Kosovo, work was continuing on the monitoring mission that was being set up in Kosovo, we have assessments of a growth of terrorist activity in Kosovo at the time, and gradually multi-ethnic forces were being introduced into Macedonia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please focus on the left-hand side of this document, the portion entitled: "The decisive force or deliberate force."

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Certain vessels are mentioned there and cruising missiles -- cruise missiles. 120 cruise missiles and 20 warships. Cruise missiles are normally vessel-borne, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, normally they are, but you can launch them from a plane of course. But these are the sort of criteria that we used, we see the number of warships, no auxiliary warships mentioned here, and the main reference, cruise missiles. So this was the situation in February 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Between the beginning of February and the end of March, was there an increase? When I say "by the end of March," I mean until the start of NATO's attack, was there an increase in warships and missiles?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not generally speaking, but the structure changed. Certain warships that were better, that were better equipped, their number increased, and the cruise missiles as well. So at the beginning of the war, the numbers were about 220 in terms of cruise missiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Admiral, what was the situation in the navy throughout the aggression?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to keep this short. The greatest concentration of the naval forces was between the 35th and the 60 days of the war, the increase having been about 100 per cent in relation to what it was in February, 35 warships, 25 vessels, 23.000 soldiers, and 660 cruise missiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What was the assessment of the effect of the naval forces on the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and how it would develop, these two seem to be some distance away from each other, don't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: No, quite the opposite is true, in fact. They're very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please slow down, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: The concentration that I talked about was closely related to the fact that forces were being introduced into Albania and Macedonia. Our assessment at the time was that it was highly likely that there would be an invasion, a ground attack that would take place in Kosovo and Metohija. So these two matters were closely related, and our assessment in the navy was that there was a high likelihood that there might be a ground attack on -- in the south-east of our coast using the port of Bar in order to introduce new forces and lend support to the ground forces in Macedonia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: We see that in the document itself, but let me ask you. The forces, the warships, the cruise missiles, this is about NATO, right? These are NATO forces, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: There are different groups being mentioned here, there is the 6th Army Fleet, which is a USA group. There are permanent NATO forces in the Mediterranean, this is STANAVFORMED group and then again you have Italian groups, Alba Due was a special one and then there's another special Italian group around the Vitorio Veneto warship.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is your information on the number of cruise missiles that were actually fired from these ships during the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: When the concentration of forces was the greatest, there was 660 cruise missiles, and according to our information about 400 of those were actually fired at various points in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Admiral, during the war you were at the Supreme Command Staff, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities there?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I was assistant Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command for the navy, and I was also the leader of the duty operations team.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: When you say "leader of the duty operations team," can you explain to the Chamber what this looked like, your term of duty, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: This was a team that would be on duty around-the-clock, and then we would take shifts every 24 hours. We would monitor closely the situation all the time throughout the VJ and throughout the entire area covered by the VJ with a special focus on the area covered by the 3rd Army in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What sort of information did you normally receive as the leader of the duty operations team?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: We received information from subordinate units through their combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you produce any documents? What were the basic documents that a team like that produced during these 24-hour shifts?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a combat report at the Supreme Command Staff level, there was a war log that was being kept, and war maps were being updated at the operations centre all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings of the collegium? How often? In what capacity? Let me ask you this, first of all: When were these held?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: In the evening hours, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were you required to attend all these meetings? What was it like really?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: I was required in a dual sense because of my capacity as the chief -- assistant Chief of Staff for the navy and as leader of the duty operations team.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, briefly: You said something about the war log. What sort of information was recorded there, or rather, you said that three types of documents were being produced: Combat reports, the war log, and the war maps.

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the order in which these documents were produced?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: The war map was being updated throughout as soon as new information was received, especially whenever a combat report was received from one of our subordinate units. Combat reports were produced based on the overall reports from all the armies and units. Having completed work on our combat reports we would draw up a war log, recording virtually only information on combat activities. This is a permanent document, which means that it is kept permanently until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: So a war log is narrower in terms of its scope than a combat report?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it records combat activity and their potential consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Admiral, let me ask you this: Based on your contribution I see that you attended a great number of collegium meetings before the war. During the war you were at the command post -- just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Some small problem with translation but we will live with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as I said, you attended numerous meetings before the war, during the war, and you took part, directly or indirectly, in the drafting of many documents that were produced by the General Staff, or rather, the Supreme Command Staff. Do you know that, or rather, do you know whether a plan of ethnic cleansing existed that would involve moving the Albanian population or expelling the Albanian population to Albania or do you have any knowledge to that effect?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard of such a plan, let alone saw such a plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: According to the estimates that the General Staff had, how many international ground forces were there that were capable of intervening in Kosovo in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, although this was not directly my line of work, I did attend the collegium meetings, so I do recall some of it. I think the estimates were around 20.000, 20.000 in the territory of Macedonia, and about 10.000 in the territory of Albania. I think that also about 3.000 members of the landing forces or air-borne forces of the Army of the United States of America, not taking into account the Siptar terrorist forces, of course, because you referred to the international forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was asking about. Now, in looking at and discussing some of the documents that you were shown, you indicated that General Ojdanic was saying that it would be imprudent or words to the effect that it would not be wise for the VJ to engage in a war or to join the war against the KLA. In one of the documents, that's the collegium minutes of the 17th of April, 1998, one of the reasons was because strategic resources were exhausted, and in another one of these minutes it was suggested that it was because the international community, as you explained, would not allow the VJ to resolve it independently. What I want to ask you is this: Was the estimation or the statement that it might be imprudent for the VJ to join the war based on the fact that the international community would intervene or that the VJ did not have sufficient resources to defeat the KLA?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I would not like to provide a focus now as to what was going on at the time, but both things were taken into consideration. On the one hand our resources were not that great and we were going into a war, and on the other hand we were clashing with the international community. So it would not be wise to do it from either aspect or both. Now, where the focus was, it's hard for me to say now whether it's the international community or the resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that according to the assessments of the VJ General Staff in 1998, you did engage the KLA and successfully executed a war against the KLA in the summer and early autumn of 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you did this with only a fraction of the budget and a fraction of the units available to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. May I explain a bit, Mr. Stamp? I just confirmed, I just said "yes," but I can provide an explanation, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, if you must.

utterances.speaker: VLADE NONKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this is not in contradiction, that is to say that we estimated that our resources were poor, and on the other hand that we -- well, that there's no contradiction involved. Quite simply, the terrorist forces had grown to such a degree that things could not be put off any longer, one had to react. And this operation, if we can call it that way, as I remember it dimly, was completed in a relatively short period of time and without the participation of international forces, or rather, a more significant participation of international forces; they did take part, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nonkovic, that completes your evidence here; thank you for coming to give it. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do have another witness, that is Colonel Milivoje Novkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give me the number, exhibit number, of his statement, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3D [In English] 1115.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether it would be convenient if we were to take the break now. There seems to be a problem with bringing the witness in. I guess that we were over-optimistic as far as the cross-examination was concerned regarding the previous witness, but the court deputy seems to be checking now, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume he's here waiting, and we have this inevitable time lapse between every witness. We've tried to do something about it, but regrettably failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Apparently he's not in the building, Mr. Visnjic, because he was scheduled to arrive later. So we will have to take the break at this stage. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I raise one issue before we do that, Your Honour. There are two exhibits proposed for use with this witness that I have an objection to based on foundation and relevance 3D735 which is entitled "NATO aggression on civilian populations and facilities in Yugoslavia." It's our position, Your Honour, I'm not sure what issue in the case it goes to and I'm not sure what this witness will be able to provide about the foundation. I think it's propaganda in our view, Your Honour, and should not be admitted, likewise for 3D737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the nature of these documents, Mr. Hannis? Are they newspaper articles? Are they pamphlets or --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There are photographs of damage partly done by NATO, pictures of victims, pictures of a head lying in the field, a picture of a small child crying. There are some videos as well. 3D737 does have -- these are basically daily reports about what is going on in the war. They will have reports about where bombings occurred and maps, et cetera, in both B/C/S and English. It appears it was prepared in both languages at the time, and that fact alone, we suggest, Your Honour, underlies our argument that it was meant in part as propaganda, the fact that it was published in English at the time the bombing was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to start with the second document. This is a war log or a war review. This is material that was prepared, and the witness is going to testify about that, and provided to foreign journalists, on the basis of which they later made requests and were allowed to visit facilities or locations that were specified in that material as well as other locations that they wanted to see. On the one hand it is a review of developments in the territory and it primarily has to do with the bombing, the air-strikes. We think that it is significant because, number one, it is a contemporaneous document; secondly, it primarily deals with facts. I think that if there is propaganda, it is only very slight. And three, this can give us a review of the strikes and the effects of these strikes on civilians and the civilian population. This review does not only include Serbia proper and strikes in that area, but also in Kosovo; that is to say, the entire territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, on a daily basis at that. As I said, all of this information was fully open to all users, as it were. Quite simply, if the Prosecutor thinks that any of this is inaccurate or is propaganda, of course he will be able to put questions to the witness in that regard. That is what I wish to say in relation to 3D737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what about 3D735?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for this other document, 735, it is -- well, it is a summary of photographs that show the degree of destruction, so that is its sole purpose, to show the effects of the air-strikes in this particular case. Again, I'm saying that it does not only pertain to the area of Serbia proper, but the entire territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, including Kosovo and other parts. Again, we would like to tender this in terms of what the effect of the NATO bombing was on the civilian population and the movements of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the link of the witness to these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness took part in preparing both documents, or rather, he was head of the service that prepared both documents. He can testify to how it was that these documents were compiled, what the sources for these documents were, what their purpose was. If Mr. Hannis thinks it was propaganda, he can cross-examine the witness about that. Finally, the witness had direct communication with many foreign correspondents, and he can even give hearsay evidence about what they experienced in these locations that are included in these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were going to say something else, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to say merely that a part of this package included set of video recordings that for technical reasons could not be uploaded to e-court, but it was disclosed to the parties. But I assume that the document as it stands would be sufficient, but we would like to tender that. But we would be guided by you. That was supposed to be part of 373 -- 737, but for technical reasons it could not be uploaded to e-court. I'm referring, of course, for the record to 3D737.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will hear the evidence as it progresses. If we feel it's inappropriate, then we will interrupt it, but on the face of it the real issue seems to be one of quality and weight. And if it is largely propaganda, then obviously that would have an impact only the weight to be given, and that's something that can be brought out in cross-examination. One thing you may bear in mind, Mr. Visnjic, is that where the events are in Serbia rather than Kosovo they may be of doubtful relevance, and perhaps you would concentrate on what's clearly relevant. These are both extensive documents and there's a limit to how much material can be considered on issues which could be peripheral if not occurring in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that it's not the right moment to provide argument, but I do have to say something about the relevance in terms of Serbia. One of the points made by the Prosecutor that Mr. Hannis tried to make through a few witnesses was related to the direction in which the refugees left Kosovo. In this way, if we show what the intensity of the bombing was in Serbia and in Kosovo, I think it will be clear that if somebody left they went to places where they would be sure that they would not be bombed. That is one point. Secondly, the question of whether people were leaving Serbia, too. I think that that is going to be part of our case at a later stage, linked to other evidence, but the first thing that crossed my mind now is what I spoke of just now. I also wish to add that the intensity of the bombing in Serbia was directly related to what General Ojdanic was doing, too, because one of his duties was- and do not forget that he was commander, or rather, Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command of the overall army of Serbia- one of the things that he had to deal with intensively was the situation in the entire territory of the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, because NATO did not declare war in Kosovo only, but in the entire territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And General Ojdanic had to grapple with the entirety of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you want us to deny admission now, do you? You're not content with a result in your favour?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no. I just want to make a comment in relation of your last observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll adjourn now and resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Novkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, is it correct that you gave the Defence team of General Ojdanic a statement on the 20th of August, 2007, and that you signed this written statement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: On your arrival in The Hague were you able to go through that statement and were you to testify before this Court would you give the same answers to the questions as indicated in that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I went through the statement and I would not have anything particular to add or to amend.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will just be asking the witness something about what my colleague Mr. Sepenuk drew my attention. In paragraph -- in paragraph 18 of the statement there may be a translation error. Let me just clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in paragraph 18 of your statement you said that: "During the NATO air-strikes a total of 25 press conferences were held and briefings." And in Serbian it says: "On the average every third day." Is that what you stated?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there is a discrepancy in the text that you have in front of you. It says "on the average three a day," that's paragraph 18 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will correct it so that it reads what has just been said by the witness, every third day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in your statement in paragraphs 16, or rather, let me first ask you: What post did you hold in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1999 I was the chief of the information section in the administration for information and morale guidance in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and at the same time I was the deputy of the chief of this administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement in paragraphs 16 through 19 you provided some basic details about the activity of your administration which is the organized provision of information for domestic and foreign media organized by the Army of Yugoslavia. Could you please tell us something more about this aspect, how this dissemination of information was actually organized.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the information provided which reflect to a good measure the activities of the Yugoslav Army press centre, I can add that when the armed aggression was launched by NATO against our country we faced a problem of how to organize a desk, some kind of a place, that would meet the requirement, the high demand on the part of the domestic and foreign reporters, and at the same time that was to be a place that we could use to facilitate to the fullest possible degree the organizational, technical, spatial, and any other requirements for the unimpeded operation and provision of objective information to the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, give me a figure or a percentage of for the foreign journalists accredited during the war in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Yugoslav Army press centre that was set up in the military centre in Belgrade, that was a place that met the requirements I was just talking about, we gave the accreditations to a total of about 2.500 domestic and foreign journalists, and out of that number about a thousand and 500 or about 60 per cent came from 490 foreign media outlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The interests of the international community for the events in Yugoslavia was quite high, I assume in light of the war.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a great deal of interest, and this was the reason why we organized this, in order to be able to provide objective and full information for all the journalists, because in light of the nature of the aggression, the Army of Yugoslavia did not have any need to hide anything, quite the contrary. It was in our own interest to -- for as many journalists to see what is happening in the field and to report on what was happening in our country as objectively as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You say that in light of the nature of the aggression the Army of Yugoslavia did not have any need to hide anything, it wanted to be open. What would the key components, the key characteristics, be of the media campaign that NATO launched against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to sum up, if we can, we could say that the media campaign during the NATO aggression against Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was primarily very broad, comprehensive, if you look at the type and number of media outlets involved. One could also say that it was very intense, if you take into account the number and frequency of the reports that were broadcast or published in that area. And in light of the character and the objectives of the campaign, it was our assessment - and I in fact still hold this opinion - that the entire information and propaganda campaign was aimed at creating an unfavourable picture of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the international community, an unfavourable picture of its state leadership and its security forces. In order to create an alibi or a justification for the causes and consequences of the aggression that was carried out, and as we all know it was carried out without a prior decision of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let me ask you something. You had about 1500 journalists?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, foreign journalists that worked with your centre, press centre. I don't know if you can -- I don't know if you can do that, but could you give us a general assessment of the way they were reporting on this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: As a whole, the journalists that were accredited by the Yugoslav Army press centre acted, generally speaking, in a very responsible manner, they were professional, and we didn't have any problems with them. They all complied with the code of their profession, but nevertheless a certain number of reporters from foreign media outlets would go into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, evading the procedure, evading the existing visa regime and the accreditation regime. They used their own channels from Macedonia, Albania, and Montenegro to get into Kosovo and Metohija, and they mostly filed tendentious reports, they usually -- that was in favour of the Kosovo Liberation Army because they were mostly, for the most part, working from within their ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you able to give us any example of a foreign journalist who wasn't accredited and may have made his or her own way into Yugoslavia and -- or into Kosovo or Albania and who reported accurately, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't give you an example, but I can -- what I can do, I can give you a different kind of example. For instance, Ms. Christiane Amanpour, a highly respected reporter from this media outlet went to Kosovo and Metohija, evading this procedure, and her coverage was mostly negative but it was very high-profile coverage, her comments were mostly negative. And I assume that there were those who reported in an objective manner in accordance with their professional code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you could name one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether perhaps we missed this question, but what were the key components of the NATO media campaign? What did NATO base its media campaign --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've already had a very long answer to that question, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I can be more specific, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just a second. Yes, your question was, you said that in light of the nature of the aggression against Yugoslavia -- sorry, that Yugoslavia did not have any need to hide anything. Then you said: "What would the key components, the key characteristics, be of the media campaign that NATO launched against Yugoslavia?" And that was answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do apologise, I did miss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: As part of this campaign that you just told us about, NATO relied on several - let me put it this way - arguments or facts that were not true in essence. Could you please list, but very briefly as a summary so that we don't get a very broad answer. What were those elements that were always stressed as facts, or rather, as arguments that would -- were put forward against Yugoslavia as part of this campaign?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the information and propaganda part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a second, please. What is the purpose of this, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to lead the witness, but if he gives an answer you will see that some of the elements that I believe were put forward by NATO during this campaign that were aimed against the Army of Yugoslavia, this is something that is first of all mentioned in the evening briefings as a response on the part of the Army of Yugoslavia or the discussion among the highest-ranking officers in the Yugoslav Army on that topic, and on the other hand some of the arguments that were put forward as part of this campaign against Yugoslavia are completely untrue by their very nature, and I believe that we will be able to prove that as our case continues. Perhaps I did not formulate this question all that well, but we're talking about a number of arguments that are being put forward throughout this NATO campaign and you will see that in various discussions, in order to get a clear clarification as to what was being debated at the evening briefings, to be quite specific now, you should know what were the accusations levied at the Army of Yugoslavia so that you can see what it is defending itself against.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I remain very doubtful about the value of this, but please continue until we see if it goes anywhere that can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please tell us briefly, really very briefly, what were the basic arguments that were used by NATO in their campaign, we're talking about facts. What did they accuse the Army of Yugoslavia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: In this campaign several untrue arguments and assumptions were put forward, and they were exploited to quite high degree in the media. Let me just give you very briefly some examples. First, that the Army of Yugoslavia is threatening to use nuclear weapons and radioactive munitions in light of the fact that in Vinca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Is this a serious example that you are going to show us collegium minutes dealing with the answer to this allegation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why are we listening to? This witness is -- he may well be an expert in propaganda. He's not here to continue that exercise; he's here to give evidence in answer to specific questions. So please control what he's doing so that we do hear relevant material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I said that I would not be showing you specific examples in the collegium meetings, I will not be doing it through this witness, but I do have specific examples that relate to what the witness just said because this is an issue raised by Mr. Stamp and Mr. Hannis with the previous witness so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Nuclear weapons being used by Yugoslavia, that was raised by the previous witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecutor asked the witness, I think it was -- well, I can't recall now who it was exactly, but somebody who attended the evening collegia, he asked him about the reactor in Vinca, whether Yugoslavia had a nuclear bomb. And one of the arguments that were put forward against Yugoslavia was that -- this thing that the witness is talking about. So he's telling us now where this information had come from initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are we going to see the newspaper in which the allegation is made?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Dead ends at the moment, Mr. Visnjic, but since the matter has been raised please continue and deal with it. Not everything you read every day in the newspaper has a -- has even the basic grain of truth in it. People are generally able to make fairly sound judgements object what might be rubbish and what might merit further attention; however, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: As for what Mr. President said --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, please, just answer those -- tell me about those theories four, five, six, and what were the basic issues in the campaign.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, apart from this theory that was published in the Washington Post, a similar thing happened with the threat of chemical weapons, that chemical weapons would be used; the next theory or argument was that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is continuing with the ethnic cleansing and has carried out an aggression in -- into the territory of northern Albania; yet another theory was that the Supreme Command Staff was deployed in a hospital, which would imply that there was a severe violation of international law of war; and leaflets were also used as one of the boldest forms of propaganda war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Now that you've enumerated all that, can I ask you whether this was made public or published sporadically in some of the newspapers or did it crop up often; and how was this information used during this campaign on the part of NATO member countries?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: The information about the ethnic cleansing of the Kosovo Albanians was a permanent feature of almost all foreign media, and as for the other theories that I just mentioned, they were -- they would be aired sporadically; and then after a few days there would be a lull.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned this theory about alleged ethnic cleansing. How did the VJ see the problem of Albanian refugees? Did you issue any communiques about this, make any announcements? Was there any reaction on your part at all?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: It was as part of our overall media analysis that we monitored this issue as well, the issue of Albanian refugees. What was typical, however, was that in terms of the way the refugees were treated in Kosovo and Metohija there was no reference to refugees belonging to other ethnic groups. The information service of the VJ analysed part of this campaign in relation to Albanian refugees, and I can say that in terms of media coverage this was hyped up as some sort of exodus and humanitarian disaster. Our take on it was that the objective of this approach was to misrepresent this to the international public in order to come up with some sort of justification for the aggression against the FRY, another objective being to mobilise the Albanian group and create greater homogeneity among the Albanians and also among the international players to mobilise them against Yugoslavia and also for --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but let me ask you a more straightforward question and we'll come back to this later. Your information centre, did you publish any announcements about the refugee problem?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: The information service of the Supreme Command Staff did not make any announcements about this specifically, but we seriously analysed this problem, we assessed the situation, and we pressed for someone from the federal bodies to address this issue, which in fact happened on more than one occasion. There was a press conference that I believe was held on the 10th of May which was dedicated solely to this issue. The army itself did nothing about this directly because we believed this to be a problem that was beyond our scope of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You said in your evidence that you had about 1500 journalists there. How did you work with them within the press headquarters, the press centre? How did you provide them with information on the combat situation and its consequences?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: It was for the benefit of all these journalists that every morning by 9.00 we would prepare and publish a bulletin, a daily bulletin we called it, providing a specific time-line of NATO air operations throughout the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This was something for them to familiarise themselves with the situation, and then it was their call whether they would eventually use the information, whether their agencies would use this information or whether they would ask to be taken to the theatre of war so that they could get some footage and write up their reports. In addition to this they had access to computers, to the internet. They enjoyed a wide TV coverage, RTS included. So on the whole I believe that their working conditions were quite fair and sufficient for them to report in an unbiased and objective manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: All right. So they received the information and then there were two options open to them. They could go on their own to particular places to produce their reports, and the other option was for you to organize their departures. In terms of procedure and method, were there any differences between these two options and were there certain restrictions imposed on journalists during trips like these?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: In more drastic cases of particularly destructive, devastating air-strikes resulting in a greater number of casualties, we would set up the entire security regime for groups of journalists to go there and see for themselves. We had convoys sometimes comprising over a hundred journalists. They could go there with no restrictions whatsoever, take their footage, talk to people, and eventually dispatch their reports to their respective agencies. There were cases, however, where certain teams belonging to certain news agencies decided to go on their own to visit certain facilities, certain areas. There had been over 720 such requests throughout the three months of aggression. We dealt with these. We made it possible for these people to go there on their own, but we would always contact a unit that would then welcome them as soon as they arrived in the area and to look after these journalists. Restrictions were only about issues that had to do with military confidentiality, subjects of a confidential nature for the military, deployment of units, perhaps some tactical manoeuvres or restrictions to do with security and safety. So these were factors that we generally took into account. We wanted to keep these journalists safe from harm, and very often in their line of work these journalists are known to come to grief in a war situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did a single journalist get killed in your area?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: There was no form of war censorship imposed by the VJ or anything like that, was there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no wartime censorship. All the media throughout the FRY were following their journalistic policies in the way they were reporting, and the information service of the VJ never interfered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you exercise any form of control over the work of these media? Did you perhaps control the work of Radio and Television Serbia throughout this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. At no point did we monitor or exercise any control over the work of Radio-Television Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: You were preparing those bulletins every morning for the benefit of the journalists, you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 3D737.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we begin with that, during the break I was handed another CD from case manager for the Ojdanic Defence which is entitled: "Addition to 3D737." So I'm not clear if this is additional material to what we were disclosed previously or not; if it is, I have a different objection than what I made before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, if I may just explain something to Mr. Hannis, the material on that CD was received previously as a 65 ter disclosure, as 737. I said that we did not have, technically speaking, an option to put everything into e-court because some of the material proved unuploadable, bearing in mind the discussion that we just had. And possibly your ruling too. I will leave this material aside for the time being. I will not be tendering any of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're making it more complicated. What's the answer to the question: Is it additional material that hasn't been produced as part of 737 or is it some part of what you've already labelled as 737?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's 737, it's part of it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And why did you hand it over just now and label it as additional material?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because only the textual component was uploaded into the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So 737 could not get into e-court, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, have you an objection to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, is it proposed to be part of the evidence? And if it's not in e-court, I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I gather it is proposed as part of the evidence, but Mr. Visnjic was going to move to something else for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may respond. At this point in time I will not be tendering this. Just to avoid any further discussion with Mr. Hannis, this will be submitted from the bar table, but this was part of the 65 ter disclosure on the 15th of June, 2007. There was a separate CD which included this material. I believe it was submitted both to the OTP and the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, please move on then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, what is it that we see before us, this document, Exhibit 737?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: It's one or two copies of this daily bulletin or review that we prepared each morning for the journalists. This was done both in Serbian and in English so that there would be no need for any translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is the title page in this case, but if we can move on to page 2 perhaps of this document and then page 3. Page 4. And finally page 5, this is the introduction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, when was the first daily war bulletin published?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have this information at my finger-tips, but it was probably five or six days after the start of aggression. We took some time to organize ourselves, and we realised that this was a necessity in order to facilitate the work of all the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
