utterances.text: So from that moment on, how often, was it published daily?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The bulletin was published in two languages, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Serbian and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you go through this document you will see that the first bulletin was published on the 4th of April from that time on until the end of war, more specifically, until the 16th, until the 18th of June, day by day, war bulletins. Can we please move to page 84 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, there is a diagram here. What were the key elements of this daily war bulletin? What did it contain?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: The key components were the time-line containing information on NATO air-strikes, targeting certain buildings and facilities, and we would also provide a diagram, or rather, a map of the FRY to show exactly what was going on so that the journalists might get a bearing. Sometimes typical photographs were included depicting the horror of war. These photographs were mostly put up somewhere in the press centre of the VJ. Throughout the aggression on two or three occasions we organized these photo exhibitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move on to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have just a question. Was this war bulletin only meant for the journalists, international journalists, who would come at the -- by a press room or whatever or was it meant for the general public? Was it circulated amongst the general public?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we saw this daily war bulletin as a document that would provide journalists with fundamental information for their work. We did not just release this to foreign journalists, though. Domestic journalists, too, had access to it but only within the perimeter of the press centre. We did not officially publish it anywhere outside the building in the form of a public announcement or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if I understood you correctly, in response to Judge Chowhan's question, if I understood your answer correctly, this war daily review was fundamental material for journalists so that on the basis of that they would write their own stories?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Or rather, submit specific requests to visit particular facilities or particular territory?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. It was not drafted as something that would be presented to the public in its final form, but it was auxiliary material for journalists so that on the basis of this material they could objectively decide what they wanted to write about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But where were -- why you didn't allow this to go to the foreign journalists? Why couldn't they have access to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you did not understand what I was saying. I said that it was primarily meant for foreign journalists, and they did receive it; however, in addition to them, others did, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, now when we look at this page here it says here: "NATO raids on civilian industrial facilities on May 4th and in the night between May 4th and 5th, 1999." From whom did you receive the information that you included in these reviews? Who was your source of information?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were several sources, primarily through the operations centre of the General Staff, that is to say in the command system. And in addition to that there were other ways, other factors that were in the defence system, civil defence primarily and other factors, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 3D735.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you are familiar with the title of this book or publication, I don't know what word to use. Tell me briefly, what does it contain?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. This is a publication from a photograph exhibition about the air-raids and the destruction of civilian facilities and economic facilities. I already mentioned that during the course of this aggression we organized such photographic exhibitions twice I think, and then finally we made a selection of photographs that were particularly characteristic. And then we published this in a single place so that journalists could use it and the wider public. We had the problem of civilian destruction and economic infrastructure destruction, and that is how we dealt with it. These are authentic photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who the authors of these photographs were? Is it one author? Several authors? Your own service? Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: There were several authors involved, and ultimately it was impossible to identify all of them because these were different facilities, different localities. There were also photographs there from our own photo service, our own press centre, but for the most part these were photographs of anonymous and other authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you, or rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to move on to another topic in relation to paragraph 20 of the witness's statement, and I would just like to ask the witness to identify a document, Defence Exhibit 3D989. As for this document, the next witness is going to speak about it in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you tell us what kind of a document this is and who issued this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is a publication, a brochure, a pocket brochure primarily meant for commanders of basic units, with a view to dealing with their knowledge of social psychology and personality psychology, refreshing it and applying it in practice in command in working with soldiers, all of this with a view to confronting fear. So that soldiers and officers could adapt to the situation more easily so that they could cope with war-related stress in a better way and so on. The publication was issued by the administration for information and morale; however, it was revised professionally by professors of Belgrade University who teach these particular subjects.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Let us move on to another topic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of that document, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we hear the next witness, then we will hear about the research he carried out in relation to fear that appears in the ranks of the Army of Yugoslavia soldiers who were in Kosovo and Metohija. This fear was an element of something that is caused, or rather, that is called morale in their terms, if I'm not mistaken, but then the witness will explain this better. So when you look at these causes of fear you will see how relevant external factors are, what it is that causes fear. You will see how and in which way, or rather, what the consequences of fear are among the population, among soldiers; that is to say among people who were not particularly trained as opposed to soldiers. We heard different evidence here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this an expert who's going to be dealing with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. He was directly in charge of the research that he wishes to present to you. So it's a document from the relevant period, this is empirical research, and the next witness is going to talk about that. Quite simply, this is not expert evidence; it is a document in this case that is from the relevant period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll deal with that problem when the witness is there. But going back to these other two exhibits, speaking for myself at the moment, I have no idea how 3D737 and 3D735 are going to assist us to determine matters of fact in this case when we've clearly indicated to you that newspaper reports are not an acceptable form of evidence, and that's essentially what these are. This is telling the journalists the information that they then put in the newspapers. And then -- and the other one with anonymous photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond to the first thing you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to the first matter, I think that the witness said what their sources of information were, and he said that the operations centre of the Army of Yugoslavia and other sources were the source of the information that he offered to the journalists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, let's have the sources. Don't give us this media propaganda machine as supposedly evidence. Use the source -- I'm beginning to wonder what your -- what it is you're actually doing here, whether you're, in fact, engaging in a bit of propaganda through the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- In relation to the history in Yugoslavia, because this -- I thought we had indicated this wasn't the way to present evidence of events. And you see the tendentious nature of the language used in this material presented to journalists also, whereas we could be seeing the reports that tell the facts. And we may even be seeing the reports, which makes one wonder why this material's here at all. I simply indicate to you at the moment, I for one would find it very difficult to give any weight to this. And perhaps we did make the wrong decision in allowing you to go down this road at all. You've a tight time-line to present solid material to us in the presentation of your defence, and this doesn't strike me, for one, as the way to use that time wisely. Anyway, let's hear what else you have to present from this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, during the course of May 1999 you were part of the team that toured the army units in Kosovo-Metohija. Can you tell us when this happened, in what period?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. Within the team of the Supreme Command Staff I was in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija from the 23rd until the 26th of May, in the command of the Pristina Corps; and after we finished our work at this command, I toured the command of the 15th Armoured Brigade and the 243rd Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. During that tour, or rather, at the end of that tour was there yet another meeting where the results of this control were openly presented?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the customary way of doing this, because there were other teams that went to other units of the Pristina Corps, and at the end it was customary to have a meeting to summarize and present the situation as it was and the observations made in these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was this meeting held to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Usually it is on the last day of the tour and the control; I think it was precisely on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell me, who was the leader of the control team?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: The leader of the control team from the Supreme Command Staff was Lieutenant-General Ljubisa Velickovic and together with him on the team was General Miodrag Simic. I was with them in the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me now, did anyone in any way, either while you were in these units that you mentioned just now or at these meetings, say to you that a number of members of the MUP and also to a certain extent smaller units as well were committing grave crimes against the Siptar civilian population in settlements, shelters, namely, murder, rape, burglary, theft, aggravated theft, and so on, and that they intended to ascribe these crimes in a premeditated fashion to members of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear this kind of assessment in any of the corps organs or in any of the units that I toured.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Colonel -- or maybe you've actually already responded to this question. I always ask witnesses this at the end. Are you familiar with any plan that the Army of Yugoslavia carried out in relation to expulsions of the civilian population from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of the existence of any such plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. You'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off except for the person who is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you now make sure your microphone is switched off, Mr. Visnjic, and any others apart from Mr. Hannis's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, the administration that you were a part of in 1998 and 1999 as I understand it was called the administration for information and moral guidance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand that in the preceding years that administration had gone through a number of name changes, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct as well, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one of the names it had in the past had been the administration for information and psychological and propaganda activities, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know why the name was changed before 1988 [sic] and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll try to answer this question as briefly as possible, although it does require a broader approach. In the briefest possible terms, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Because of the events in the former SFRY in 1990, because the one party system was abolished and because Yugoslavia broke up, the former political administration from which all those organs or names stemmed, it was not viable anymore as such and it had to undergo functional and other transformations. And that is how, in particular 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994, things were going in all directions and you saw that I explained some of that. And then in -- sometime in 1994, again as part of this process of transforming the military and in an effort to depoliticise the army, we came up with this term which is similar to the terms and names used in other armies for such units, and that was how it was defined in effect. But quite soon we realised that this component, the psychological propaganda activities, was something that we were not good at, that we didn't really have capabilities for it. And the original idea for the most part was to have the defensive component, as it is called, in order to set up a system to protect the army personnel against modern psychological activities. So that was the concept, that was the approach. But quite soon we abandoned that, we realised that moral guidance or morale as an expression of the combat spirit in -- of the troops is something that is unavoidable, and that's why we came up with this name. It was transformed again as the -- and it became the administration for morale. I was no longer there and I think that it functioned for a while and then it was abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 I take it from paragraph 12 of your statement that the administration for information and moral guidance had four organizational units, including a department for psychological and propaganda activities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 13 of your statement it -- you list the basic functions of the administration. And about two-thirds of the way down the page I see the functions include: "To organize a system of psychological and propaganda activities in order to protect VJ members from enemy psychological and propaganda activities and offensive PPD," which is the acronym for psychological and propaganda activities,"against the enemy." So that's correct, you -- you were trying to deal with protecting your own VJ members from propaganda from the other side, but it was also part of your job to create offensive propaganda against the other side, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, but in the redistribution of all those functions, the emphasis was placed on the defensive component and very little focus -- in fact, it depended on the need - was placed on the other one. We never really developed it. According to the wartime establishment, we could have set up those units, too, but we simply never did establish this offensive component.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Defensive and offensive don't mean a lot to me in this context, I'm afraid, and the answers do appear confusing. Can you assist, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With the different -- and also is it possible to deal with the question of is it moral guidance or is it morale we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I think moral is typed where it should be morale, but moral guidance could pertain to morale in my understanding, Your Honour. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, Colonel, as I understand it, and I'm trying to follow-up on the question the Judge just posed, defensive propaganda, you're really talking about how to help your soldiers deal with the kinds of propaganda that they might be hearing from the other side, in this context NATO and Radio Free Europe and Deutsche Welle and the propaganda they might be hearing in foreign media or in seeing in leaflets dropped by NATO. Is that what you're talking about when you talk about the defensive activities of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think your interpretation is quite fair. I have nothing to add to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think now that I read the answer again it is clear. It was something that was abandoned, but -- it was something unavoidable and they returned to it, so I think I understand now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me follow-up just to I'm clear, Colonel. Then the offensive activities in this case would be your side, the VJ army and the Serb side in this conflict, trying to put out information or propaganda that would either make NATO want to abandon the fight or make the international community put pressure on NATO because of how they perceived what NATO was doing in Serbia. Would that be an example of the offensive propaganda?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I would dare to suggest that these two documents, 3D735, which is entitled: "Trace of inhumanity," and 3D737, the daily briefings, are, at least in part, examples of offensive propaganda. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree because we provided this to the reporters, who would then assess themselves whether there were any elements to use this document as a basis from which to work. So I can't really see how this can be qualified in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In fairness to you, let's break it down into two parts because I think there's a stronger argument as to one of the documents rather than the other. Let's talk about 3D735, which is the publication, the book, that is mostly photographs, and it's calls: "Trace of Inhumanity." I'm looking at page 5 of the document and it says this was I guess published by Vojska Publishing Information Centre, special editions department. So that's a -- that's an in-house publishing body in the army, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Vojska Publishing Centre, that was part of, or rather, it was an organizational unit of our administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is -- this indicates this is the 3rd edition published in 1.000 copies. Do you know how many editions there were in total? I take it there were two earlier editions of this; do you know when they were published?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Those editions were a result of an exhibition that was put up by the military, and probably after this exhibition a selection was made and photographs were put together and this publication was published after that. I don't know how many editions there were. I don't think, in fact, that there were any other editions apart from this one that you're quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you think this one which is called the 3rd edition is the only edition; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it's the only one. I guess there have to be the first one and the second one, but I don't think that any editions were put out after this one, after the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. And to whom were these given? Were they sold or were they given away? How were they distributed?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Those publications were not sold. They were displayed at the desk of the Yugoslav Army information centre. Anyone could take them and use them as they see fit -- as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I thought you had said earlier that one of the purposes of this publication was to help the reporters in writing about the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I said that about daily overview, that was its main purpose, but this publication, quite specifically, did not serve that function.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would agree with you. I think this publication was intended to and did serve the purpose of offensive propaganda against NATO, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you, with this assessment, because it was not intended for that. That was not its function. It painted a realistic picture. It was an overview of the destruction caused to civilian and business infrastructure. I can't see how it could have been used as offensive propaganda against NATO, whose member states have much better developed psychological operations and who have much better methods of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't see how portraying pictures of body parts and small children crying could have a positive offensive propaganda effect against NATO? Isn't that why this publication was created?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't do it in order to do propaganda work against NATO, but simply to show the consequences, the destruction, the suffering of the victims. And if we can talk about the propaganda aspect, then we can only talk about it within the context of the defensive component that I was talking about, to build the unity among the people, to motivate them for the defence. That's the way I see it. Secondly, I apologise, all the photographs are authentic, they're true. There are witnesses to corroborate what is shown on each and every one of them, authentic testimony, so I can't really see how that could be used as offensive propaganda activities against NATO, except for this element that I mentioned to present to the domestic and international public what actually is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I would suggest that there are certain kinds of propaganda. Good propaganda is the kind that can serve both purposes at the same time. It serves the defensive purpose of uniting the VJ soldiers because they're outraged at seeing these kinds of photographs, which suggests that these crimes have been committed by NATO against their families and their people, and at the same time it could cause outrage in the international community or help widen the gap that may have existed among all the NATO parties about this bombing campaign. So this book is an example of the kind of propaganda that serves both purposes, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you heard the question, Mr. Novkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand the comment and I can partly agree with it, but not with the conclusion. Mr. Prosecutor, that was the raw truth, the reality. We wanted to show this to the people, that was our aim, and that we were building a national unity on victims, on destruction. And what you're characterizing and offensive propaganda aimed at our population, and in particular at NATO, that's not something that I can accept. And I'm quite amazed because no one has ever levied any such accusation at us from the reporters, from the international community, nobody has ever labelled this as propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'd be surprised if that turns out to be correct. I want to ask you about the photographs. You said they're all authentic and all true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if this is the time for the break or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We'll take a break right now, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Novkovic, we do have to have a break at this stage, that will be for half an hour, and we shall resume at 6.00. Could you meanwhile leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, before the break we were talking about Exhibit 3D735, the book called: "Trace of Inhumanity." And earlier at page 62, line 4, in your answer you indicated that all these photographs are authentic, they're true, there are witnesses to corroborate what is shown on each and every one of them, but I thought I heard you say earlier in response to a discussion about this book that some of these photographs were anonymous, is that correct, are there some of these photographs that you don't know where they came from?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I may have said that, yes. But, if I may correct myself, that is not quite what I meant, anonymous. Perhaps it was the case that I didn't know who the author was, as simple as that. But as for the editorial board and the publishing operation itself, I suppose they have records on each and every photograph. Therefore, I have to correct my previous statement. Perhaps I did say anonymous, but we didn't just pick those randomly. As far as I'm concerned, I really didn't know at the time who the authors were of each and every photograph that we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at the exhibit and look at page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I have a question for you about this. I think the first photograph on the inside next to the editorial information and it simply saying: "Yugoslavia, wartime spring, May 24th 1999." Do you have any idea what this is a photograph taken of, where it was taken, by whom? You don't know, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but you're pushing me into a corner here and making me answer questions that I'm unable to answer. I wasn't in charge of that myself. It wasn't my job; however, it's perfectly easy to interpret what the photograph itself shows. Anyone can see that for themselves. It's about sorrow, it's about pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. I would suggest to you it's propaganda intended to unite your soldiers and to make NATO lose support in the international community, both defensive and offensive propaganda purposes, correct, because it's not for informational purposes. There's nothing about it except Yugoslavia, spring, and a date, so it's certainly not for informational purposes, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't quite agree. This photograph informs the public about the pain and suffering of our people, the civilians. If you really think that it can make a Yugoslav airlines pilot cry and make him give up his professional responsibilities, well in that case, yes, perhaps you might choose to call it propaganda. The simple fact is I don't agree, especially the part where you talk about an offensive component.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll take it that you don't agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at page 96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 65, I'm not sure if the witness said Yugoslav airlines, because that's what the transcript says, I don't think if that's what the witness said. If you really think that it can make a Yugoslav airlines pilot cry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] NATO, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the translation we have is: "If you really think that it can make a Yugoslav airlines pilot cry ..." Now, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness said JAT, J-A-T.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have misspoken. What I had in mind was NATO because they were the ones carrying out the air-strikes obviously. Thank you for this correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You appear to have said JAT, J-A-T.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible. Probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we look at page number 96 of this exhibit, please. Well, perhaps my page numbering is wrong. I think I have to go back two pages from this item for a paragraph. It's page number 94. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, what about this photograph, it has no caption at all. Can you tell us anything about who that's a picture of, when it was taken, where it was taken?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't provide this kind of information simply because I was not directly involved and it wasn't possible for me to obtain that sort of information. It may have been an omission on the part of the publisher. I think this information should have been clearly stated; however, one can see what the photograph itself shows. It's crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I think it's crystal clear what its intended to show, I agree. Let me ask you about the -- one of the other jobs of your administration. I think in page -- or at paragraph 12 you mentioned the department for culture and tradition and the Vojska news and publishing centre was linked to that department, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the publishing and information centre, Vojska, was one of the organizational units of the moral guidance department. There was the army museum, the military history institute containing the military archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did the army department for culture and tradition focus primarily on Serb culture and tradition?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just Serb culture and tradition. In practical terms we used that department to organize certain features in the VJ, and this included all of its members. We nourished the traditions and culture of each and every ethnic minority present within the VJ because we were the VJ. The whole of Yugoslavia was included, and we followed this principle with no exceptions. We were very consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999, what percentage of the VJ was composed of soldiers and officers of the Serb ethnicity? Wasn't the army at that time a substantial majority of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the military or the professional?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, tell me about the professional first.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: The professional set-up to a large extent reflected the overall ratio between Serbs, Montenegrins, and ethnic minorities in the FRY. It was, roughly speaking, within those boundaries in terms of the presence and involvement of the overall population of the FRY. I do have to mention this, though, there were no Albanians or next to none, and their involvement certainly didn't reflect their share in the overall Yugoslav population. As for the military set-up, the situation was more or less similar, but again I have to point out that members of the Albanian minority boycotted the VJ and boycotted to a large extent their regular military terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that because of that boycott and that underrepresentation of Albanians in the army, that the army didn't spend much time talking about Albanian culture in the department of culture and tradition?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, no restrictions were imposed by us on the Albanian ethnic minority or, indeed, their culture. As for active features, shows, every time there was something organized in the way of arts and crafts, there was never any restriction on a show or a feature being shown from that particular area and belonging to that particular culture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about paragraph 19 of your statement, and this has to do with the journalist and credentials that were handed out. You told us and I think you testified that there were some 1.535 credentials issued to journalists from 490 foreign media. Can you tell us from what area those countries were? Did you hand out any credentials, for example, to reporters from the United Kingdom, from Australia, New Zealand, or the United States?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: There were journalists from the countries you mention as well. I can say that journalists from all over the world were represented. There was enormous interest. There were journalists from South America, Australia. Given the amount of interest, it was precisely the way you say it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mention Christiane Amanpour you wouldn't have given her a credential, would you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: At the start of the air-strikes, she was in Belgrade, she was accredited, she was working there for some time. For some reason, I think in mid-April, she left of her own accord. She took a route out through Hungary and Budapest and all of a sudden, as soon after, she turned up in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Isn't a possible explanation for that because she wanted to get an objective view from the other side rather than just the information that was being provided to you -- by you to the foreign press?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: That could be one possible interpretation, but considering the visa regime that applied in the country, considering her accreditation that had been granted, I think a fair thing to do for her would have been to simply request that and I'm sure we would have accommodated her and made it possible for her to go to Kosovo and Metohija. Additionally what happened is that at long last she accessed Kosovo and Metohija, which was our territory, illegally, and then she did what she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Visnjic asked you about some of the NATO propaganda or the -- the untrue things that were being said about you that you had to confront and deal with. You mentioned that one of the -- one of the primary things was the theory or the argument- this is at page 41- that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is continuing with the ethnic cleansing, and are you saying that there was no truth to that at all or that it was exaggerated?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: We should distinguish between ethnic cleansing and refugees. There were refugees. There is no doubt about that. In my view, if I may, I can tell you what the reasons were for the existence of refugees and for the fact that their numbers grew up to a level where it was eventually termed an exodus or a humanitarian disaster. First of all, I think the refugees convoys, not to the same extent of course, came about already in 1998, as early as that, because of combat activity by our security forces as they were fighting Albanian terror groups. Their lives were at risk, and there was pressure on the population in those areas. I believe that to have been one of the reasons. This occurred as early as 1998. Secondly, the steep increase in the number of refugees in Kosovo and Metohija occurred when the air-strikes were started. There were many agencies in the western world that conveyed statements made by Albanians who were part of those convoys, clearly showing that it was the NATO air-strikes that caused them to flee and be afraid for their own safety and that of their families, which eventually increased the number of refugees. Next - this is my own personal view but this is also based on some analyses and inferences that can be made - the increase in the number of refugees, which is what eventually happened, was part of an organized media campaign, another kind of campaign, being launched by certain players in the west. There were refugees on both sides. What I have been talking about here for the most part was about media manipulation and media misrepresentation and misuse of this problem of refugees. I never challenged that because there were refugees belonging to almost each and every ethnic group present in the area. For the most part, they were Kosovo Albanians naturally because they are the predominant population in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's true, Colonel. Would you allow for the possibility that one of the reasons for those thousands of Albanian refugees -- Kosovo Albanian refugees leaving Kosovo, as testified to by a number of them in this trial, was that they were forced out by forces of the Serbian MUP and by the army, according to their testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to confirm that. I can't describe it in that way. It is possible that in certain areas where combat operations and clashes were continuing, especially in 1998 when the fighting was fierce, certain groups were taken away from those areas or taken to safety. But I really have no information indicating that this was done solely on account of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned the daily briefings and you prepared your daily bulletins, I guess you called them, for the journalists. And I think you said at line -- page 42, line 25, you provided a specific time-line of NATO air operations throughout the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This was something for them to familiarise themselves with the situation, and then they could decide on their own what they wanted to do about it. But in those daily bulletins you were not providing the journalists any information about combat operations being carried out by the VJ in support of the MUP or in coordination with the MUP and anti-terrorist operations against the KLA. You weren't giving them that information, were you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in this form that you mentioned, as part of the daily bulletin, but we did organize press conferences. We did issue public statements. The information service of the Supreme Command Staff did. We had a total of about five press conferences throughout the aggression, and we published about 35 public announcements. There were five press conferences, and these focused most of all on combat operations. And also when they toured units, they had a chance to see for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And these daily information reports on the NATO bombing, they didn't include every target that NATO had bombed, did they, but only those that you had selected to put in the daily bulletin, right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Not every target was included, because then the bulletin would have had to run into several pages. A selection process was needed and there were a couple of people who were in charge of that. A time-line needed to be provided for these combat operations, but the principal idea was to prioritize the targets, to prioritize also in terms of destruction levels and casualties. Our selection was geared towards the most severe cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 48, line 21, you said that this was auxiliary material for journalists so that on the basis of this material they could objectively decide what they wanted to write about. But I suggest to you that there's a limitation because since you're doing - and by "you" I mean the army and your unit - you're doing an initial screening process so that they could write about anything that you had initially screened and then spoon-fed to them. Isn't that right? You've preselected what they can choose from?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: The daily bulletin was supposed to be used in some sort of a reference point and the -- the editors and journalists were free to use it as they saw fit. They may have had other sources of information and neglected the daily bulletin altogether. They could have requested to go and take shots of a entirely different target or facility. We always tried to accommodate any such requests. As I mentioned before, I think we dealt with over 700 such requests that were made on individual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Visnjic then asked you about what was your source of information for the facts you were putting in the bulletins. You mentioned there was several sources, primarily the operations centre in the General Staff. I want to know, sir, did you also get -- or did you also use information that you heard in the -- in the daily Supreme Command Staff briefings that you attended? Did you sometimes use that information in the bulletins?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: You could say that, yes. I attended briefings every day at the Supreme Command Staff. For the most part, information on combat activities was sent through the operations centre and the command system. In addition to that, as I mentioned already, we used other sources such as civil defence sources, civil protection sources. Objectively speaking, it wasn't possible to use only the command system to register every single time a target was hit and every single time a combat operation took place. So we used this information network in the civil protection system too. We used information from local media as well because they, too, were providing information, but we would check and verify every single thing, every single bit of information before it was included in the bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you then providing only information about the NATO bombing or were you -- I thought you -- I understood you to say before that you were providing other information about the conflict in Kosovo, not just the NATO bombing targets. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: We were providing other information, too, but the overview of NATO air-strikes on civilian and industrial targets had the major share. But we also spoke about the taking down of such planes as F-117 and F-116 fighter planes. We also included other information -- other information occasionally that we believed might be of interest to the journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's have a look at Exhibit 3D721, and if we could first go to page 2 of both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Colonel, I would tell you this is a briefing of the staff of the Supreme Command on the 3rd of April, 1999, which apparently started about 8.30 in the evening. I think you told us you attended every session from the 1st of April on through the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Every session for the most part. Sometimes I was away on official business controls and such, sometimes I was not at the Supreme Command Staff. On those occasions, I didn't attend, but I did attend most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to look at the paragraph in B/C/S on the page in front of you it's the paragraph that begins right after the one that has the number 2.000 in it. And in English I'll read you how it's translated. It says: "With regard to the territory, there are problems with paramilitary formations. Intelligence has it that there are volunteers who have arrived in Kosovo and Metohija without the army being aware of it, and these are the MUP reserve forces." And then there's a proposal: "Inform MUP and other organs to undertake measures within their competence." And finally a reference to: "A group of 32 volunteers was sent back from Kosovo and Metohija. Seven looted," and then it's incomplete. And finally the next one is General Ojdanic speaking. The prior comments I can tell you from the preceding page came from Colonel Gajic. And General Ojdanic here says: "The command of the 3rd Army is to explain why these 32 were together and not in the units." Do you recall this being discussed at that meeting about problems with volunteers and ...

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I personally cannot remember specifically from this particular collegium, but I do have reason to believe that it was the way you said it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, that was not the kind of information you were putting in the daily bulletins, was it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That kind of information we did not put in the daily bullets because -- well, as I was saying, this review could not have been that succinct and it could not have been as functional as we wanted it to be. We wanted it to be there to assist the journalists in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to page 5 of the English, and I believe it is page 4 of the B/C/S. Colonel, this is the same briefing and this is General Ojdanic sort of -- it looks like summing up at the end of the meeting. And under number 18, item 2, it says: "Prepare denials on refugees (administration for information)." Do you recall what that was about? I will tell you in the first page of this meeting General Krga mentions that they claim there are about 500.000 refugees, so I assume he's referring to NATO when he says "they" there. Does that help you recall what this was about?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying that I don't know whether I specifically attended that collegium meeting, but I remember that practically as for the problem of refugees, Albanian refugees, as this was present in the public all the time, we always examined that problem -- well, always, I mean to the extent to which we pointed this out as a permanently present problem in the international public. Then I understood General Ojdanic to say that this should be dealt with, denied, a denial should be issued from the federal government. You know why? You know why there was this problem with the issuing of these denials, what it boils down to as far as we in the military are concerned? The media were saturated with all these figures that were being bandied about. There was a race going on. The figures varied to such an extent, tens of thousands, and there were even high officials who stated that it was over 1 million, 1.2 million, 1.3 million, that is why we thought and that is why it was the position of the collegium that somebody should speak up and say what the truth would be in approximate terms, in terms of actual figures. We were not denying the fact that there were Albanian refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But here it does say "administration for information," that would have been you and your -- your administration, your department, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The tactical mainstay involved is issued with a task and the moral guidance --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. I'm running short of time and I want to try and finish you today so you can go home. If you can give short answers where I ask a question for a short answer, that will help.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page of the B/C/S and keep the English page that we have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, the next one will be item number 20, and this again is General Ojdanic talking. And now I'll read the English to you. It says: "Colonel Novkovic to see to it as to what information is needed for work of the press centre in the VJ club and no other information is to be supplied by anybody else. All assistants are to be briefed as to what information should be announced." Were you aware of that? Whether you were present at the meeting or not, were you aware that that was what General Ojdanic had said?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I was present at this meeting. We thought that it was only natural because in all well-regulated systems, especially in the military, the army is a well-regulated system, there is a system of subordination and we thought that that was indispensable in order to preserve the system of command. This warning was there in order to prevent improvisation, also wilful behaviour on the part of individuals, because there were such attempts too --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: -- And attacks at units themselves in terms of jeopardizing the security and safety of the units themselves and of journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is also to control the flow of information, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. As for lower commands, we did not carry out any corrections in terms of their press releases and the information they provided. We just wanted this to be within a single system in terms of coordination and in terms of appropriate assistance, otherwise we did not correct anything, and we did not exercise any immediate influence unless something drastically went against the grain of soldierly norms or threatened the system of military secrets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying that during the war the lower units, for example, the 3rd Army, the Pristina Corps, the 243rd Brigade, issued their own press releases about what was going on without any review or control from above? Is that what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: They had a high degree of independence in view of the assessments, the situation, the substance that they were trying to get across. We just coordinated things, if necessary, also in terms of giving them some assistance to convey what it was that they were releasing. They have a rather high degree of autonomy in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So they weren't required to submit their press releases for approval to you or some higher body before they went out? That's what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how often, if you know, was the 3rd Army or the Pristina Corps issuing press releases? On a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: It was not on a daily basis. It was only natural that they were in the focus of everyone's interest and the greatest pressure of journalists was precisely aimed at that command and those units. As for their relations with the public and the information they provided, they combined it with several -- in several different forms. Statements made by the commander of the 3rd Army or the corps commander or some other organ from the command or through press releases or through clips at the RTS or through other media, so it was combined. Methods were combined. And also those who spoke in public varied, those who provided information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From what I've seen and heard about the VJ, it seems like this was a -- this was a well-organized army. There must have been some rules or regulations controlling what could be said, what could be released in press releases by the 3rd Army or the Pristina Corps or subordinate units; that's correct, isn't it, limitations on the kind of information that could go out?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I understood you correctly, you are talking about a general principle that exists in all armies in the world. So from that point of view one could say that that was the way it was in our army. However, due to the dynamic of combat activities and everything that was going on, we could not fully exercise such a principle. On the other hand, we thought it was necessary that the public should be made aware of what was going on in that war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would those rules be found in the VJ rules of service if I were trying to find them or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I think that that provision can be found in the rules of service. I cannot remember exactly which particular article, but I think that this was regulated in normative terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally could we look at item 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the English translation says: "On Monday in the VMA meeting room, review the defence plan again in case there is a land operation." Can you tell us what the VMA meeting room is?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that these are perfectly normal, official premises. I personally think that apart from this official room that is used every day for these everyday meetings, it's nothing else, it's nothing else. There is no special room as far as I am aware at the VMA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What does "VMA" stand for?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: It means the military medical academy, Vojno Medicinska Akademija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's where the army hospital is located as well in Belgrade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in actual fact, that is a specialised military hospital; however, with the status of a research institution. So it has different clinics, poly-clinics, institutes. So it is a hospital, but a very high-level hospital that also engages in scientific research.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that reference is to a meeting of the collegium that was held on the 9th of April, 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that that is that collegium. I also attended it; however, I think that the choice was made to have it held at the VMA because the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command with his collegium wanted to pay a visit to the military medical academy, or rather, the patients there who were in hospital at the time. But as far as I can remember, it was nothing special, it was regular type of meeting, without anything special about it, just that one single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't remember that that was a marathon session of the VJ collegium where the situation in the republic after the first 17 days of the NATO air-strikes was discussed at great length and there were concerns expressed about the storage of resources and supplies, I can't remember if it was General Kovacevic or General Krga talked about might only have enough to carry on for another seven to ten days of the war. And at the end of that session, a directive was drawn up for how to deal with the upcoming days in the war. You don't remember April 9th as being a special meeting, a long meeting with hours spent dealing with having an analysis and writing up assessments which General Ojdanic said that he was going to take to the Supreme Command the next day? You don't recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that meeting. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were there, Colonel, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's the one, but in my view it wasn't a marathon meeting, as you had put it, as it was not presented that way either as far as materiel reserves and resources were concerned and the situation in the Republic of Serbia was not characterized as dramatic. Within the scope of my own authority, and that was following the situation regarding morale in the army, I was a member of the collegium, but I personally do not recall such descriptions and characterizations and I don't really have the impression that it was a meeting that was that long, a marathon-type meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Colonel, we have that document in evidence. I don't have the time to go through it with you now because I want to ask you about Exhibit P2941. And I'm sorry, sir, I don't have this in Serbian. I have English. And these are some media reports in which you are represented as having made certain comments. I'll read it to you in English and ask if you remember speaking about this. The first one is from page -- starts at the bottom of page 28 of Exhibit 2941. It's from Belgrade Radio Beograd Network it's entitled: "FRY army spokesman denounces NATO's intensified attacks." And I want to go over to page 29, actually, at least in my copy and I go down to where it says: "Begin Novakovic recording ..." The first part I want to ask you about relates to the number of Albanians in Kosovo, because you mentioned that that was a matter of some dispute. Sir, you're attributed as saying: "So the number of over 1.5 million Albanians who lived in Kosovo and Metohija is still being manipulated with completely inaccurately and arbitrarily. Over 800.000 of them have allegedly left the area. It's also being claimed without any grounds that the remainder of the 600.000 Albanians are hiding in the hills and woods, allegedly out of constant fear of the Yugoslav security forces. Claims are being made -- also being made about alleged mass executions in the villages and towns in Kosovo and Metohija. The facts, however, show something different. The truth lies in the following: The number of Albanians in Kosovo and Metohija did not exceed 800.000." Can you tell us where you got our figures from, that in 1998 and 1999 the number of Kosovo Albanians did not exceed 800.000? What was your source?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I used the federal government as a source, their Ministry of Information. For the most part they used that figure, of 800-something thousand Albanians, 200-something thousand Serbs, Montenegrins, Yugoslavs, and so on and so forth. On the whole this is what the official statistics was. The figure that was being bandied about was 1.4, 1.3 million, but that is the source I used primarily. It was an official source in a way. They did rely on certain estimates and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to go to the bottom of the page. This is another topic, again attributed to you saying: "The headquarters of the Supreme Command energetically denies this loathsome lie. We absolutely reject any thought that the Supreme Command Staff of the Yugoslav armed forces could threaten the security of sick and wounded persons with any move and endanger the regular functioning of this respectable and internationally recognised health constitution. The military medical academy in Belgrade is a highly specialised scientific medical institution in which both military and civilian persons, as well as foreign citizens, are being treated with equal care." And you go on to say: "Those who know this or should know it would never place the General Staff of the army that was victorious in the Balkan and both world wars in a hospital. In addition to the preposterousness of such tricks, this and similar lies demonstrate the absurd attempts by the aggressor to undermine through well-established military propaganda the unity of the Yugoslav Army and the unity of people in the defence of their country." Now, this was you speaking to rebut the claim that the Supreme Command had been based or had been meeting in the military medical academy, and the fact is it had met in the military medical academy at least once for that collegium session on the 9th of April, 1999. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, probably, but I guess it's a mistake in the translation because I never said undermining our propaganda. I don't really see where this construction comes from. This was probably an attempt made by the information service to tell the international public and the public at home that in keeping with military tradition the General Staff and officers will never abuse the military hospital. And it is from that point of view that I made this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, I suggest that you weren't being truthful when you acted with outraged indignation to the suggestion that the General Staff had been meeting in the military hospital. That's correct, isn't it? You didn't tell them the truth when you made that denial?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not a meeting at the VMA that is referred to here. What is being said here that -- is that the General Staff is deployed at the military hospital, and you must admit that the difference is drastic. The collegium could have been held somewhere else at a military school, at the military museum, wherever, but it just so happened that this time it was held at the military medical academy, but it certainly wasn't deployed there and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do have some questions. Please, this same Prosecution Exhibit, I can't see what it is, I can't see the number, 2941. I see the page here, K0541233. Could I please have K0541231, that is to say two pages before this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, Mr. Hannis was a bit unfair to you. Now I'm going to show you this very same document and please pay attention to the date when it was that you made this statement. Colonel, when was this statement made about the Supreme Command and the Supreme Command Staff not being deployed or based in the military hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: What I see before me is the 16th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm asking you the following. Do you know that between the 9th of April and the 16th of May at any time any meeting of the military or state leadership was held at the military medical academy and whether they were deployed there or based there at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: After this collegium that was referred to, the 9th of April, that is, as far as I know and on that basis I claim that not a single meeting of the collegium of the Supreme Command Staff was held at the military medical academy. So this denial I issued here had to do with the statement that the Supreme Command Staff was deployed at the military medical academy and that was functioning from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let me ask you something. If the Supreme Command Staff had really been based at the military academy, would the hospital have been a possible legitimate target in terms of what you know concerning the rules of war and warfare?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the rules, if such a facility is abused by the military, then it does become a legitimate target.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could you please look at 3D735 now. While we're still on this topic, the military medical academy and so on, could you please tell me, what was the basic purpose of General Ojdanic's visit and the visit of members of his collegium to the military medical academy on that day?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: The basic purpose of that meeting was to actually visit some of the wounded army personnel there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have 3D735.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis showed you page 4 of this document. This shows -- this is a photograph of some persons, there is no caption.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown pages 9, 10, and 11, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, below each of these photographs there is a caption. What does it say by and large?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't see because it's too small, but -- well, it says here Aleksinac - I have the English version here. So you have the location, you have the picture, the picture speaks for itself, and there is a description of what it is all about underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 11, 2 now. Could we have the next page, please. And the one after this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Could you please pay attention, there is a date here on the next page, yes. Again, we have the location and the date.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJE NOVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 94. And could we please have page 93. 92.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And 91 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Page 93 shows the Dubrava prison in Istok. If we're going to show that I want to move to re-open our evidence about Dubrava prison rather than what's shown in that caption to that photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not my intention to show anything about Istok, but I just wanted to show that underneath each photograph there is a caption containing either the location or the date or both the location and the date and the identification of the person. What Mr. Hannis did is to show the witness the first photograph and the last photograph in this book. If you go through the whole book you will see that every photograph has to do with a certain location. In some cases there is also a reference to a date and to a name. So it is very easy to verify whether such an incident really happened, the one that is depicted on the photograph. Well, Istok is really on this photograph by mere chance. It was not my intention to bring it in any way in the context of the indictment or things that are at dispute here. So in this document that contains about 90-so pages, except for the first page which is, in fact, just the cover and the last page, which is again some kind of a cover, in most cases a photograph has at least a reference to the location, in most cases there is a reference to the location, date, and the name of the person that was involved in the incident. And since now I actually replied instead of the witness, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I repeat what I said earlier, Mr. Visnjic, and I make the point on my own behalf, but I find it very difficult to see the probative value at the moment in these pictures even with what's said in them. I find it difficult to see that they're any different from the press reporting that we've encouraged you to avoid utilising as evidence in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Novkovic, that completes your evidence here. Thank you for coming to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what's happening tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know we have a videolink set up for tomorrow, two witnesses, first General Geza Farkas and then General Andjelkovic. And, Your Honours, if we may move into private session for just a moment, not more than ten seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall sit at 9.00 tomorrow -- sorry, is tomorrow 2.15? Oh dear. Clearly my fault. I have a list here. So we'll sit at 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of September, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.07 p.m.,
